stops.title: The question
stops.text: So far every paper has made the model faster by shrinking its weights. This one takes a different road. Tri Dao asks why attention is so slow on a GPU, and how close it can get to the speed of a plain matrix multiply. His answer is that attention is held back by memory traffic and by poor work splitting, not by arithmetic. FlashAttention-2 gives exactly the same output as ordinary attention, only about two times faster than the original FlashAttention. No approximation, no retraining.

stops.title: Same maths, less traffic
stops.text: Here is the core idea in one picture. On the left, standard attention computes the full score matrix, N by N, writes it to slow GPU memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the probabilities, and reads them again. On the right, one fused kernel streams small tiles of queries, keys and values into fast on-chip memory and writes only the final output. The extra memory drops from N squared to N. That was the first FlashAttention. Version two keeps this idea and asks what still wastes time.

stops.title: Two speed gaps
stops.text: Two gaps on the A100 explain the whole design. First, the big main memory is roughly ten times slower than the small on-chip memory, and the original FlashAttention already avoided that. Second, the Tensor Cores do matrix multiplies at 312 teraflops, while operations like exponentials, maximums and rescaling run at only 19.5. So one of those small operations costs about sixteen matrix multiply operations. Because of this, and because work was split badly across the chip, version one reached only 30 to 50 percent of peak.

stops.title: Softmax one tile at a time
stops.text: Before the fix comes the trick that makes tiling possible at all: the online softmax. A softmax normally needs the whole row, but here each row keeps a small running state, its current maximum, its running sum, and an unnormalised output. Each new tile updates the state, and when a larger maximum appears, the old contributions are shrunk accordingly. After the last tile the result is exact. FlashAttention-2 makes one small change here: it postpones the division by the sum to the very end, which saves costly non-matmul work.

stops.title: Swap the loops
stops.text: Now the heart of the paper. In version one, the outer loop ran over key and value tiles, so every query block had to read its partial output from main memory and write it back at every step. FlashAttention-2 swaps the loops. The outer loop runs over query blocks, and each block keeps its running state in fast registers until it is finished, then writes once. Notice that the output does not change at all. Only the order of work changes, and the expensive rescaling mostly disappears.

stops.title: Fill the whole chip
stops.text: The swap has a second benefit. Query blocks are independent, so they can run in parallel. Version one only split work over batch and attention heads. With long sequences the batch is usually small, so only a few of the A100's 108 processors had anything to do. FlashAttention-2 also splits along the sequence, so every processor stays busy. Inside each block it also divides work between warps so they no longer have to exchange partial sums. Notice that batch one generation, the case in this project, is exactly this situation.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: This chart shows the speed-up over the original FlashAttention, forward plus backward, across sequence lengths. With head dimension 64 it is about 1.6 to 1.8 times, and with head dimension 128 about 2.3 to 2.5 times. The gain is largest exactly where version one was weakest, which supports the diagnosis. The forward pass alone reaches about 73 percent of the A100's peak. The caveat: these are hand-written CUDA kernels on Nvidia hardware, so treat the numbers as qualitative for Intel.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what does the thesis take from it? A video transformer attends over all its space and time tokens at once, and attention cost grows with the square of that count. NNCF weight compression does nothing for attention, because attention has no weights. So the job is to verify, not to implement. The check is that the exported LTX-2.3 graph contains OpenVINO's fused scaled dot product attention nodes, and then latency is measured with and without them. Next, DeepCache speeds things up differently, by reusing features across denoising steps.
